cover.alt: At the shop counter in the morning, Ser Bindo holds a small book open with a gold florin lying on one line; Lapo stands beside him with the big ledger.
cover.art_brief: Florence, a grey February morning in 1300, inside the Cerchi company's shop near the Cerchi houses: a long wooden counter, bales of wool and folded cloth behind. Ser Bindo, an old bookkeeper in a dark notary's gown, holds open a small leather-bound book; a gold florin lies flat across one line of writing, covering a name. Lapo, sixteen, lean and dark-haired, in a plain tunic, stands at his elbow beside the big open ledger and looks at the coin, not at Bindo. Ink outline and restrained watercolour wash. No legible text, lettering, numbers or captions anywhere.

words_with_history.title: Dal latino all'italiano
words_with_history.text: Il mercante deve avere trenta fiorini, e la lana deve dare trenta fiorini. Cento soldi fanno cinque lire.
words_with_history.note_en:
Florence used medieval units with Latin names. The libra (a pound weight) gave the lira, the solidus (a late-Roman gold coin) the soldo, and the denarius (the silver penny) the denaro. The medieval system counted twenty soldi to a lira and twelve denari to a soldo, the same ratios as the old British pound, shilling and penny (£ s d: libra, solidus, denarius). By 1300 these were mostly units of account; the coin in a merchant's hand was often a gold florin, whose value in soldi moved. Two of the words widened: denaro and the plural soldi now mean simply "money".

The verbs of the ledger are Latin too: dare is dare, avere is habere and dovere is debere. Habet → ha and debet → deve lose the final -t. Italian has devono and the older literary debbono (formed like debbo < debeo); devono is the ordinary modern form. Comprare continues late Latin comparare, which had come to mean "procure, buy" (classical Latin buys with emere). Deve dare and deve avere are what Latin would say with debet dare and debet habere: "must give" (owes) and "must have" (is owed).

A pattern to recognise, not a rule: Latin b between vowels often corresponds to Italian v (habere → avere, debere → dovere). Libra → lira is an exception: the b was lost before r, where -br- normally gives -bbr- (fabrum → fabbro, febrem → febbre). Pagare descends from Latin pacare, "to pacify", through the later sense "to satisfy a creditor"; in Italian it means "pay", not "pacify".

grammar.note_en:
**The present, all persons.** Bindo's lesson needs every person: «Oggi scrivi tu» (today you write), «Scrivo: Monna Cilia deve dare dieci fiorini» (I write: Monna Cilia owes ten florins), «Da una parte scriviamo chi deve dare» (on one side we write who owes), «Voi scrivete tutto due volte?» (do you write everything twice?), «I Cerchi comprano lana e vendono panni» (the Cerchi buy wool and sell cloth). The endings continue Latin ones: io -o (scribo → scrivo), tu -i (scribis → scrivi), the third person without its -t (scribit → scrive, debet → deve), voi -ate/-ete/-ite (-atis/-etis/-itis: contate, scrivete). Two things are new. Noi ends in -iamo in every class (compriamo, vendiamo, scriviamo): the -iamo of the old subjunctive spread to all verbs. In the third plural, Latin final -t disappears and an -o is added after the surviving -n: comparant → comprano, vendunt → vendono. There are three classes, by the infinitive: -are (comprare, contare, trovare), -ere (scrivere, vendere, leggere) and -ire. Many -ire verbs insert -isc- in the singular and the third plural, the Latin inchoative -sc- (florescit → fiorisce) here a mere filler with no sense of beginning: capire → capisco, capisci («Capisci?» «Capisco, messere»: Do you understand? I understand, sir). Other -ire verbs take the endings without -isc- (Latin audio, audis → Italian -o, -i); the first of them comes in chapter 3.

Table key: io trovo, scrivo, capisco (I find, write, understand); tu conti, scrivi, capisci (you count, write, understand); chi compra, vende (whoever buys, sells: Bindo's «Chi compra deve dare, e chi vende deve avere», whoever buys owes and whoever sells is owed); noi compriamo, vendiamo (we buy, sell); voi contate, scrivete (you count, write); i Cerchi comprano, vendono (the Cerchi buy, sell).

The examples in full: «Da una parte scriviamo chi deve dare, e dall'altra chi deve avere» (on one side we write who owes, and on the other who is owed); «Voi scrivete tutto due volte?» (do you write everything twice?); «Noi dobbiamo dare trenta fiorini, e il mercante deve avere trenta fiorini» (we owe thirty florins, and the merchant is owed thirty florins); «Ma prima devi capire una cosa» (but first you must understand one thing); «Voi due, che cosa fate? Contate i panni o guardate Lapo?» (you two, what are you doing? are you counting the cloths or watching Lapo?); «Allora dovete contare, non guardare» (then you must count, not watch); «Anche noi possiamo mandare un giovane a Roma» (we too can send a junior to Rome); «Oggi nessuno» (nobody, today).

**Irregular verbs** are learned as words, as in Latin: fare (io faccio, voi fate: I do, you do; le due parti fanno la stessa somma, the two sides come to the same sum), andare (chi va a Roma, whoever goes to Rome; i pellegrini vanno, the pilgrims go), venire (il denaro viene da qualcuno, money comes from someone; vengono cento pellegrini, a hundred pilgrims come), dire (che cosa dici?, what are you saying?; dico che il libro non torna, I say the book does not balance), sapere (io non lo so, I don't know; non lo sai, you don't know it; il vecchio non sa più contare, the old man can't count any more), dare (la compagnia dà venti fiorini, the company gives twenty florins; il papa dà il perdono, the pope grants the pardon). Dà has an accent to tell it from the preposition da.

**Dovere, potere, volere + infinitive.** As debeo, possum and volo take an infinitive, so do their Italian heirs: devo domandare (I must ask), devi capire (you must understand), dobbiamo dare (we owe), dovete contare (you must count), devono fare il cambio (they must change money); posso scrivere (I can write), puoi guardare (you may look), chi va a Roma può avere il perdono (whoever goes to Rome can have the pardon), possiamo mandare (we can send), i soci possono fare (the partners can do); voglio sapere (I want to know), che cosa vuoi dire? (what do you want to say?), Ser Bindo vuole sapere (Ser Bindo wants to know), volete mandare (you want to send), i soci vogliono una tavola (the partners want a table). Potere and volere change their stem, as dovere does (devo, deve; dobbiamo, dovete): posso, puoi, può; voglio, vuoi, vuole. Posso is possum and può is potest, almost unchanged. Dovere still means both "must" and "owe", and Bindo's book uses both at once: deve dare, "must give", is the debit (he owes); deve avere, "must have", is the credit (he is owed). The plot turns on two modals: alone with the book, Lapo thinks «Io posso scrivere l'altra parte» (I can write the other half), and then «Ser Bindo vuole sapere perché: allora devo domandare» (Ser Bindo wants to know why: then I must ask).

**Questions and negation.** Questions need no particle; the question word comes first: chi (who: Chi deve avere?, who is owed?), che cosa (what: Che cosa scrivi?, what do you write?), quanto (how much: Quanto fa da una parte?, how much is it on one side?), perché (why, and also because: Perché due volte, messere?, why twice, sir?), per quanto tempo (for how long). Non before the verb negates a clause on its own: non guadagniamo (we do not earn). It also goes with mai, niente and più placed after the verb, unlike Latin, where nemo or nihil stands alone: Ser Bindo non scrive mai male (Ser Bindo never writes badly), noi non perdiamo niente (we lose nothing), il vecchio non sa più contare (the old man can no longer count). Before the verb, or alone, nessuno needs no non: nel libro nessuno deve dare (in the book nobody owes), «Oggi nessuno» (Nobody, today).

**Lo, la, l' before the verb.** A few object pronouns come before the verb: «Lo leggono i soci» (the partners read it), «Quello che non vedi, non lo sai» (what you don't see, you don't know), «tu non l'hai mai visto» (you have never seen it; l' = lo before a vowel). They are chapter 3's subject. Non l'hai mai visto is also a passato prossimo ("have seen"), the tense of chapter 4; here it is one fixed warning.

**Present for future.** As in colloquial English: «Domani voglio sapere se il libro torna» (tomorrow I want to know whether the book balances), «Paghiamo fra un mese» (we pay in a month's time).

**Numbers and money.** The prose writes numbers in words. Lapo's sums: cento soldi, cinque lire (a hundred soldi, five lire); centocinquanta lire, sessanta fiorini o più (a hundred and fifty lire, sixty florins or more); trenta e dieci, quaranta (thirty and ten, forty). Like chapter 1's «dieci e trenta fa quaranta», «trenta e dieci fa quaranta» is spoken reckoning with a singular fa. Twenty soldi made a lira, and twelve denari a soldo. The gold florin floated against them, at very roughly forty to fifty soldi in 1300, so 150 lire (3,000 soldi) were sixty florins or more. Dal latino all'italiano gives the names' history.

**Tu and voi.** Voi is both a plural and the respectful singular. Bindo's «Voi due, che cosa fate?» (you two, what are you doing?) is a plural; Lapo's «Voi scrivete tutto due volte?» to Bindo and Bindo's «Avete ragione, messere» (you're right, sir) to the partner are respect.

**Fact and fiction.** Boniface VIII proclaimed the Jubilee in the bull Antiquorum habet of 22 February 1300, backdated to Christmas 1299. It offered full pardon to the penitent who had confessed and visited the basilicas of St Peter and St Paul, on thirty days for Romans and fifteen for others. The Spini were among Boniface's chief bankers. The Cerchi shop, Monna Cilia, the partner and the twenty florins are invented. Double entry was new in 1300 (the Farolfi ledger of 1299–1300 is an early example), and partners' secret books (libri segreti) are attested in Florentine companies; Bindo's rule is his own practice, a little ahead of many shops.

A.title: A
A.instruction: Write the present of the verb in brackets, in the person the sentence needs. Block 1: dovere and potere before an infinitive. Block 2: other verbs.

C.title: C
C.instruction: Questions 1–2: answer in Italian or English, in your own words, then compare with the model. Questions 3–4 are Dal latino all'italiano: question 3 in Italian, question 4 in English or Italian. (3) A Latin account book would say: Mercator debet habere triginta florenos. Domina Cilia debet dare decem florenos. Write the two lines in Italian, as Bindo dictates them. (4) Debere means both 'owe' and 'must'; habere means 'have'. Explain why, in Bindo's book, deve dare means 'owes' and deve avere means 'is owed'.

items.prompt: Che cosa trovò Lapo nel libro grande, la sera dei conti?
model_answers: Trovò una partita di Ser Bindo: venti fiorini a un messere, con solo una lettera del nome, e l'altra parte non c'era.
items.rubric: Totalling the month alone, Lapo found an entry in Bindo's hand: twenty florins to a 'messere' whose name is only one letter. He looked through the whole month and the month before and found no other half: nobody 'deve dare' those twenty florins, so the book does not balance. He thought of writing the other half himself, wrote nothing, and decided to ask. An English answer is fine.

items.prompt: Perché Ser Bindo mise un fiorino sul nome?
model_answers: Per mostrare a Lapo l'altra parte, ma non il nome di quel messere.
items.rubric: Bindo wants Lapo to see that the entry has its mate (the same day, the same twenty florins, in the partners' libro segreto), so that the two sides reconcile; but the man who received the money must stay unnamed. The gesture shows it, and so do his words, «Puoi guardare la partita. Il nome no.»; he carries the book away with the florin still on the name. (His «Questo, ragazzo, non lo devi sapere» answers a different question: why the company pays the man.) An English answer is fine.

model_answers: Il mercante deve avere trenta fiorini. · Monna Cilia deve dare dieci fiorini.
items.rubric: Mercator → il mercante (with the article Latin lacks); debet → deve; habere → avere; dare stays dare; triginta → trenta, decem → dieci; florenos → fiorini (both masculine plural here); Domina Cilia → Monna Cilia: Monna < madonna (mea domina), the title of a respectable woman. Word order is Bindo's: who, then deve dare or deve avere, then the sum.

model_answers: Monna Cilia ha il panno, e deve dare dieci fiorini. Il mercante dà la lana, e deve avere trenta fiorini.
items.rubric: Debet dare is 'he must give': the person has received something (cloth, money) and must give its value, so he owes: the debit. Debet habere is 'he must have': he has given something (wool) and must receive its value, so he is owed: the credit. Bindo's rule: chi compra deve dare, chi vende deve avere; and every sum is written on both sides.

notes: Chapter 2 of design v4, written by Claude Opus 5.5 from plan/cards/ch02.md in the parallel wave (chapters 2-7). Draft; no audio; one cover and one margin diagram planned, nothing generated.

Story choices inside the card's beats: the 'cash book' of card scenes 3-4 is not named, because cassa is chapter 7's word. Lapo finds the twenty-florin entry in the libro grande, and Bindo's rule names «nel libro grande, in questo libro o in un altro libro della compagnia», which leaves room for chapter 13's libro della cassa (after Codex review). The card's 'hand over the name' becomes a florin laid on the name, since mano is chapter 4's. The recipient's name in the big book is one letter («Del nome c'era solo una lettera»). Lapo considers writing the missing half himself and does not: a quiet plant for the forged line of chapter 12. Bindo's rule is given in chapter 13's words, «Ogni partita vera ha la sua compagna».

Words owned by later chapters were written around: madre, mano, aprire, chiudere, cassa, riga, prova, notizia, voce, cercare, portare, aspettare, compagno, vero. Two single glossed incidentals are declared for the quoted rule: vera (vero is chapter 3's) and compagna (compagno is chapter 4's; chapter 13 needs the bookkeeping sense «mate»).

Lexemes: 49 new, within the ceiling of 80: the 48 planned items plus partita (entry in an account book; used by chapter 13), each used at least three times. Held deltas (chapters 8 and 15) already date the planned words to it-dante-01-l02 and carry no base card stages or entry-level receptive_only for them, so no held entry needed changing; their sense ids are copied here. Chapter 1 lexemes with forms first used here: contare (contate, contiamo), guardare (guardate), falso (falsa).
Chapter 1 words recycled as OPEN.md asked: ricco 2, povero 2, falso 3 (with falsa and the gloss vera ↔ falsa), sole 2, monna 4 (Monna Cilia), giorno 15, sera 3.

Shared files changed (for integration): course.json bridge_references.la appended statim, mittere, verbum, iubilaeus, venia, relinquere, loqui, tempus, debet, litterae, possumus, pecunia, emere, incipere, mensa (all real Latin with the sense used); names_personal + Cilia; place_chunks + San Pietro, San Paolo; function_words + centocinquanta (level 2); lessons row l02 now has path and published false. glosses/forms.json: 53 new form entries; 'torna' now lists present 3sg (comes back; of accounts, balances) before the imperative.

Length: 1,391 running words, at the top of the advisory window (1,000-1,400; checker target 1,200 plus or minus 15%): the lines added after review carry G02 persons inside existing beats (volete, vogliono, possono, puoi, vuoi); none is padding.

History: the bull Antiquorum habet, 22 February 1300, backdated to Christmas 1299; fifteen days' visits to St Peter's and St Paul's for non-Romans, thirty for Romans, with confession (Treccani, Giubileo; Senato exhibition 'Antiquorum habet'). The Spini as papal bankers (Treccani DBI, Spini). The florin at very roughly 40-50 soldi in 1300 (Treccani, fiorino); Lapo's «sessanta fiorini o più» for 150 lire (3,000 soldi) holds anywhere in that range. One lira = 20 soldi = 240 denari.
